Summary: Create a .NET 10 class library named WordCounter that exposes a public static class WordCounter.WordCounter with a public static method CountWords(string input) returning the count of words in the input, where a word is defined as a maximal contiguous run of Unicode letters or digits (per char.IsLetterOrDigit semantics), per human decision specification-001.
Requirements: The solution must be a .NET 10 class library project.
The assembly/project must be named WordCounter.
The library must expose a public static class named WordCounter in the WordCounter namespace, fully qualified as WordCounter.WordCounter.
The class must expose a public static method with signature: public static int CountWords(string input).

A word is defined as a maximal contiguous sequence of one or more characters that are letters or digits, using Unicode-aware classification (equivalent to char.IsLetterOrDigit) rather than an ASCII-only [a-zA-Z0-9] definition. This includes accented letters, non-Latin scripts (e.g., Cyrillic, CJK), and non-ASCII decimal digits as valid word characters.
Any character that is not a letter or digit under the Unicode-aware classification (including whitespace and punctuation) acts as a separator and is not counted as part of a word.
Consecutive separator characters between words are treated as a single boundary (do not produce empty words).
If input is null, CountWords must throw ArgumentNullException.
If input is an empty string (""), CountWords must return 0.
If input consists entirely of whitespace, CountWords must return 0.
If input consists entirely of separators (non-alphanumeric characters under Unicode-aware classification, including whitespace/punctuation) with no letters or digits, CountWords must return 0.
AcceptanceCriteria: CountWords("abc123") returns 1 (letters and digits together form a single word).
CountWords("abc-123") returns 2 (hyphen is a separator, splitting into two words).
CountWords("  leading and trailing  ") returns 3 (three maximal letter runs, "leading", "and", and "trailing", separated by whitespace).
CountWords("word1\nword2\tword3") returns 3 (newline/tab characters act as separators).
CountWords("café") returns 1 (the accented Unicode letter 'é' is classified as a letter, per Unicode-aware classification decision specification-001, so 'café' is a single maximal letter run).

CountWords("naïve???42") returns 2 (the accented letter 'ï' is part of the Unicode letter run "naïve"; the three '?' characters are punctuation and act as separators, splitting "naïve" from the digit run "42" into two distinct words).
The WordCounter.WordCounter class and CountWords method are accessible as public static members from outside the assembly.
OpenQuestions: Should apostrophes within words (e.g., "don't") be treated as separators (yielding two words) or is there any special-casing needed? Assumption: apostrophe is not a letter/digit, so it acts as a separator ("don't" -> 2 words), per the stated definition with no exceptions.
